questions.q: What does a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerability allow an attacker to do?
choices: Read arbitrary files from the web server's filesystem
Induce users to perform actions that they do not intend to perform
Execute arbitrary SQL against the application's database
Decrypt the victim's session cookie offline
questions.explain: CSRF lets an attacker induce a user to carry out an unintended action, partly circumventing the same-origin policy.

questions.q: Which three conditions must be in place for a CSRF attack to be possible?
choices: A relevant action the attacker has a reason to induce
Cookie-based session handling (the app relies solely on session cookies to identify the user)
A cross-site scripting flaw on the same page
No unpredictable request parameters the attacker cannot determine or guess
The victim must be using an outdated browser
questions.explain: The three conditions are: a relevant action, cookie-based session handling, and no unpredictable request parameters.

questions.q: CSRF can only arise with cookie-based session handling and never in other contexts.
questions.explain: Although normally described with cookie-based sessions, CSRF also arises wherever the app automatically adds credentials to requests, such as HTTP Basic authentication and certificate-based authentication.

questions.q: If a sensitive action can be performed with a GET request, how might a self-contained CSRF attack be delivered without an external site hosting a form?
choices: By sending the victim an encrypted email attachment
With a single malicious URL on the vulnerable domain, e.g. an pointing at the action URL
By poisoning the victim's DNS cache
By brute-forcing the session cookie
questions.explain: A GET-based action can be triggered with a single URL, for example .

questions.q: The delivery mechanisms for CSRF attacks are essentially the same as for reflected XSS.
questions.explain: Typically the attacker hosts malicious HTML on a site they control and induces victims to visit it (via a link, email, social media, or a comment on a popular site).

questions.q: Why is CSRF described as a "one-way" vulnerability while XSS is "two-way"?
choices: CSRF works only over HTTP while XSS works only over HTTPS
With CSRF the attacker can issue a request but cannot read the response, whereas XSS can issue requests, read responses, and exfiltrate data
CSRF affects only GET requests while XSS affects only POST requests
CSRF requires two victims while XSS requires one
questions.explain: CSRF can induce a request but cannot retrieve the response; XSS can issue arbitrary requests, read the responses, and exfiltrate data to an attacker domain.

questions.q: CSRF tokens protect against stored XSS vulnerabilities.
questions.explain: CSRF tokens do not protect against stored XSS. If a CSRF-token-protected page is the output point for stored XSS, the payload still executes when a user visits the page.

questions.q: How can an attacker use an exploitable XSS flaw to perform an action that is itself protected by a CSRF token?
choices: By guessing the token through a timing side channel
The injected script can request the relevant page to obtain a valid CSRF token, then use that token to perform the protected action
XSS automatically disables all CSRF token checks
By replaying the victim's previous token from the browser cache
questions.explain: Because the attacker's script runs in the victim's context, it can fetch a page to read a valid token and then submit the protected request with it.

questions.q: In general, how do the consequences of XSS compare to those of CSRF?
choices: CSRF is generally more serious because it can read responses
They are always identical in severity
XSS is generally more serious; CSRF often applies only to a subset of actions while XSS can induce any action the user can perform
CSRF is more serious because it bypasses the same-origin policy entirely
questions.explain: XSS consequences are generally more serious: CSRF often covers only a subset of actions, while a successful XSS can induce any action the user can perform.

questions.q: An application validates the CSRF token on POST requests but skips validation for GET. How can this be bypassed?
choices: Send the token twice in the POST body
Switch the request to the GET method, which is not validated
Remove the session cookie from the request
Base64-encode the token value
questions.explain: If validation depends on the request method, the attacker switches to GET (e.g. GET /email/change?email=...) to skip the token check.

questions.q: An application validates the CSRF token only when it is present. What is the correct bypass?
choices: Send the token parameter with an empty value
Send the token parameter with a value of 0
Remove the entire parameter containing the token (not just its value)
Send a malformed token that fails parsing
questions.explain: If validation is skipped when the token is omitted, removing the whole token parameter (not just blanking its value) bypasses the check.

questions.q: If a CSRF token is not tied to the user's session but accepted from a global pool, an attacker can log in with their own account, obtain a valid token, and feed it to the victim.
questions.explain: When tokens are validated against a global pool rather than the user's session, any issued token is accepted, so the attacker supplies one of their own.

questions.q: When a CSRF token is tied to a non-session cookie (e.g. a separate csrfKey), what additional capability does the attacker need to exploit it?
choices: The ability to read the victim's session cookie
Behavior that lets the attacker set a cookie in the victim's browser
Admin privileges on the target application
A valid TLS client certificate
questions.explain: The attacker obtains a token and its matching csrfKey cookie, then uses cookie-setting behavior to plant that cookie in the victim's browser and feeds the matching token in the attack.

questions.q: The cookie-setting behavior used to exploit a token-tied-to-cookie flaw must exist within the exact same web application as the CSRF vulnerability.
questions.explain: Any other application within the same overall DNS domain can be leveraged to set a suitably scoped cookie, e.g. staging.demo.normal-website.com setting a cookie read by secure.normal-website.com.

questions.q: In the "double submit" defense (token duplicated in a cookie and a request parameter) with no server-side state, why can an attacker succeed without obtaining a real token?
choices: The server derives the real token from the session cookie
They can invent a token, use cookie-setting behavior to plant it as the cookie, and submit the same value as the parameter so the two match
The browser automatically signs the token
Double submit is immune to CSRF
questions.explain: Validation only checks the parameter equals the cookie, so the attacker invents a value, plants it in both the cookie and the request, and the match passes.

questions.q: In the context of SameSite cookies, how is a "site" defined?
choices: The exact scheme, domain, and port
The top-level domain plus one additional level of the domain name (TLD+1)
Any domain sharing the same IP address
The full hostname including all subdomains
questions.explain: A site is the TLD (e.g. .com) plus one more label, i.e. TLD+1; scheme is also considered when deciding same-site.

questions.q: A cross-origin request can still be same-site, but a same-origin request cannot be cross-site.
questions.explain: A site (scheme + TLD+1) is broader than an origin (scheme + domain + port). So two URLs can differ in origin yet share a site; same origin always implies same site.

questions.q: Under SameSite=Lax, which conditions must both be met for a cookie to be sent in a cross-site request?
choices: The request uses the GET method
The request resulted from a top-level navigation by the user (e.g. clicking a link)
The request includes a valid CSRF token
The request was initiated by a script or iframe
questions.explain: Lax sends the cookie cross-site only for top-level navigations using GET; it is not sent on cross-site POSTs or background requests from scripts, iframes, or image references.

questions.q: Which SameSite restriction level means the browser will not send the cookie in ANY cross-site request?
choices: None
Lax
Strict
Secure
questions.explain: SameSite=Strict withholds the cookie from all cross-site requests, so it is only sent when the target site matches the site in the address bar.

questions.q: A cookie set with SameSite=None must also include the Secure attribute, or browsers will reject it.
questions.explain: SameSite=None disables SameSite restrictions but requires Secure, so the cookie is only sent over HTTPS; otherwise the browser rejects the cookie.

questions.q: How can a SameSite Strict restriction be bypassed using an on-site gadget?
choices: By using a server-side redirect from the attacker's site
By finding a client-side redirect that builds its target from attacker-controllable input, producing a same-site secondary request that carries the cookies
By setting SameSite=None on the attacker's own cookie
By sending the request over HTTP instead of HTTPS
questions.explain: Browsers treat a client-side redirect's resulting request as an ordinary standalone same-site request, so it includes all site cookies. A server-side redirect does NOT work, since the browser still sees the original cross-site origin.

questions.q: Some frameworks (e.g. Symfony) allow a CSRF attacker to bypass Lax restrictions on a POST-only action. How?
choices: By sending the POST body as JSON
By using a GET-method form with a _method=POST override parameter that takes precedence for routing
By adding a Referrer-Policy header
By duplicating the session cookie
questions.explain: A top-level GET navigation includes a Lax cookie; a _method override parameter then makes the framework route it as a POST, performing the sensitive action.

questions.q: What does the HTTP Referer header contain, and what is a notable quirk about it?
choices: The server's hostname; it is required on every request
The URL of the page that linked to the requested resource; it is an optional header and is misspelled in the HTTP spec
The victim's session token; it is always encrypted
The user's IP address; it cannot be modified
questions.explain: Referer holds the URL of the linking page, is optional, and is famously misspelled in the HTTP specification; linking pages can withhold or modify it.

questions.q: An application validates the Referer only when it is present. What technique drops the header so the check is skipped?
choices: Adding Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url
Including a <meta name="referrer" content="never"> tag on the attack page
Appending the target domain as a query string
Using the POST method instead of GET
questions.explain: A META referrer tag set to never causes the browser to omit the Referer header, bypassing validation that is skipped when the header is absent.

questions.q: Which of the following can bypass naive Referer validation?
choices: Placing the expected domain as a subdomain of the attacker's domain (e.g. vulnerable-website.com.attacker-website.com) when the app checks the Referer starts with its domain
Placing the expected domain elsewhere in the URL (e.g. attacker-website.com/csrf?vulnerable-website.com) when the app only checks the Referer contains its domain
Encrypting the Referer header value
Removing the session cookie
questions.explain: Prefix checks are defeated by crafting a subdomain; substring/contains checks are defeated by putting the domain elsewhere in the URL.

questions.q: Many browsers strip the query string from the Referer by default. How can an attacker force the full URL (including query string) to be sent?
choices: Set the Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url header on the exploit response
Set SameSite=None on the attacker's cookie
Use the _method override parameter
Add a <meta name="referrer" content="never"> tag
questions.explain: Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url (spelled correctly here) ensures the full URL, including the query string, is sent in the Referer.

questions.q: According to the guidance, which criteria must a CSRF token meet?
choices: Unpredictable with high entropy, like session tokens
Tied to the user's session
Strictly validated in every case before the action is executed
Stored in a cookie for convenience
questions.explain: A proper CSRF token is unpredictable/high-entropy, tied to the session, and strictly validated every time. Tokens should NOT be transmitted in cookies.

questions.q: CSRF tokens should be transmitted within cookies for simplicity.
questions.explain: CSRF tokens should not be transmitted within cookies; a typical secure approach is a hidden field in a POST form.

questions.q: Why is placing a CSRF token in the URL query string considered less safe than a hidden form field?
choices: Query strings cannot be read by JavaScript
The query string is logged in various places, may leak via the Referer header, and can be displayed on-screen
Query strings are always sent over HTTP
Query strings cannot hold enough entropy
questions.explain: The query string is logged client- and server-side, is liable to leak to third parties in the Referer header, and can be shown on-screen in the browser.

questions.q: CSRF token validation should be performed regardless of the HTTP method or content type of the request, and a request with no token should be rejected the same as one with an invalid token.
questions.explain: Server-side validation must compare the request's token to the session-stored value in every case, independent of method or content type; a missing token is rejected like an invalid one.

questions.q: What SameSite policy does the guidance recommend using by default for cookies?
choices: None, for maximum compatibility
Lax, since it is the browser default
Strict by default, lowering to Lax only with good reason, and never None unless the implications are fully understood
No SameSite attribute at all
questions.explain: Use Strict by default, lower to Lax only when necessary, and avoid SameSite=None unless you fully understand the security implications.

questions.q: Properly configured SameSite restrictions are completely powerless against cross-origin, same-site attacks.
questions.explain: SameSite only distinguishes sites, so it gives no protection against same-site, cross-origin attacks; isolate insecure content (like user uploads) on a separate site and audit sibling domains.
